passages.title: Grandmother's cup
passages.text:
Last Saturday, Malika decided to make bread for her family. Her grandmother usually bakes it, but this week she was visiting Malika's aunt in another town. Malika found her grandmother's recipe in an old notebook: "500 grams of flour, two cups of warm water, a little salt and some yeast."
She weighed the flour on the kitchen scale. Then she took a big tea mug from the shelf and used it as her cup. She mixed everything in a bowl, but the dough was very wet and sticky. It looked like soup.
Malika was worried, so she called her grandmother and read the recipe to her. Her grandmother laughed. "My cup is the small blue one on the top shelf," she said. Malika found the small blue cup and started again. This time the dough was soft and smooth, and the bread came out of the oven golden. At dinner, her little brother ate three pieces.

passages.title: A message from Timur
passages.text:
Hi Sardor,
Thanks for your message. We are all happy that you are coming to stay with us next week!
I have some news about Saturday. Your train now arrives at ten o'clock, not at nine, because the timetable has changed. I can't meet you at the station because I have a football match in the morning, but my mum will be there. She will wait next to the ticket office. She has a red bag, so you can find her easily.
On Sunday, we want to go to the mountains with Dad. It is cold there in the evenings, so please bring a warm jacket and good walking shoes. Don't bring a towel – we have lots.
Call me when you get on the train!
Timur

passages.title: School library: new rules
passages.text:
From Monday, the library will open at 8:00 and close at 17:00. On Fridays it will close early, at 14:00, because the librarian has a teachers' meeting.
Students can now borrow three books at a time, not two. You can keep them for two weeks. If you need a book for longer, ask at the desk before the two weeks end.
The upstairs room is now a silent room. Please do not talk or use your phone there. If you want to work with friends, please use Room 3, next to the entrance.
The library has four new computers. Book a computer at the desk. Each student can use a computer for one hour a day.
Lost a book? Tell the librarian. Please do not buy a new one before you talk to her.

passages.title: The wrong bus
passages.text:
Bekzod usually goes to school by bike, but on Tuesday it was raining hard, so he took the bus. He did not know the buses very well. He saw a blue bus with the number 18 and got on. After ten minutes, he looked out of the window. He did not see any shops or houses that he knew.
He asked the driver, "Does this bus go to School 21?" The driver shook his head. "No, you need the number 8. This is the 18." Bekzod got off at the next stop. An old woman at the stop showed him where to wait for the number 8.
When he arrived at school, his first lesson had already started. He told his teacher what had happened. She listened and smiled. "Well, now you know two bus routes," she said.

passages.title: Kamola's idea
passages.text:
Every summer, Kamola helps her uncle Rustam at his fruit stall in the town market. This year she noticed something. Many older customers wanted only two or three apples, a few apricots and a small bunch of grapes, but her uncle sold everything by the kilo. Some people looked at the prices, shook their heads and walked away.
One evening, Kamola told her uncle her idea: they could put different fruits into small paper bags and sell each bag at one fixed price. Uncle Rustam was not sure. "People come to the market to choose their own fruit," he said. "They don't want someone else to choose for them." But he agreed to try it on Saturday, the busiest day of the week.
Kamola prepared thirty bags on Friday night. By eleven o'clock the next morning, every bag was gone, and several customers asked if there would be more next week. Her uncle didn't say much, but on Sunday he bought a hundred paper bags and asked Kamola to make a sign for the stall in her best handwriting.

passages.title: My phone-free hour
passages.text:
I used to take my phone to bed every night. I told myself I was just checking messages, but often I was still watching videos an hour later. In the morning I felt tired, and I found it hard to concentrate in my first lessons.
Last month I decided to try an experiment. Every evening at ten, I put my phone on the kitchen table, far from my bedroom. The first few nights were difficult. I kept thinking that I was missing something important. To fill the time, I started reading a novel that my sister had given me two years ago. I had never even opened it.
After about a week, things began to change. I fell asleep more quickly, and I didn't need three alarms to wake up. I also finished the novel, and I've started another one.
I'm not saying phones are bad. I still use mine a lot during the day. But for me, the hour before sleep is now for books, not screens. My friends laughed when I told them about my experiment. Now two of them are trying it too.

passages.title: A letter to a sports centre
passages.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing about the swimming course for teenagers at your sports centre, which my sister and I joined in September. When we paid for the course, we were told that there would be no more than ten students in each group and that lessons would last one hour. However, there are now eighteen students in our group, and because the pool is shared with another class, our lessons usually finish after about forty minutes.
I understand that the course is popular, and our teacher, Mr Karimov, is excellent. He tries hard to help everyone, but with so many students he cannot watch all of us properly. Last week my sister waited at the side of the pool for almost ten minutes before she had a turn.
I would like to ask whether it is possible to divide our group into two smaller groups, perhaps by adding a lesson on Saturday mornings. If this is not possible, I think we should receive part of our money back.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours faithfully,
Dilshod Ergashev

passages.title: The interview
passages.text:
Sevara had never had a job interview before, so she prepared carefully. She read about the café on its website, practised answers to common questions with her older brother, and chose her clothes the night before.
The manager, a tall woman called Mrs Nazarova, did not ask any of the questions Sevara had practised. Instead, she gave Sevara a tray with four glasses of water and asked her to carry it across the busy room to a table by the window. Halfway there, a little boy ran in front of her. Sevara stopped suddenly, and one glass fell onto the floor and broke.
Sevara's face went red. She apologised, put the tray down, found a cloth behind the counter and started cleaning up before anyone asked her to. When she finished, she picked up the tray again and carried the other three glasses to the table.
Back in the office, Mrs Nazarova smiled. "Everyone drops a glass sometimes," she said. "I wanted to see what you would do next." Sevara started work the following Monday.

passages.title: In praise of being bad at something
passages.text:
For most of my school years, I only did things I was good at. I joined the maths club because I had won the class competition, and I avoided the art room because my drawings looked, as my younger brother kindly put it, "like maps of nowhere". It seemed obvious: why spend time on something when you will never be the best at it?
Last year a friend persuaded me to join a beginners' choir. I cannot really sing. At the first rehearsal I was so worried about being heard that I mostly just moved my lips. But something unexpected happened over the following weeks. Because nobody expected anything from me, including myself, I stopped thinking about results and started paying attention to the music itself. I noticed how the different voices fitted together and how a single wrong note could change the feeling of a whole line. For the first time in years, I was learning something simply because I enjoyed it.
This has changed how I approach the subject I am good at. In maths, I used to feel a kind of panic whenever a problem did not open up immediately, as if my identity were at stake. Now I treat a difficult problem more like a new song: something to explore slowly, with mistakes as part of the process rather than proof that I am failing.
I am still a weak singer, and I probably always will be. But I have come to think that everyone should have at least one activity in which they have no reputation to protect. It is surprisingly freeing.

passages.title: The wooden box
passages.text:
Javlon's father had repaired watches in the same small workshop for twenty-five years. The shop sat between a bakery and a phone shop, and on most days the smell of fresh bread was stronger than the smell of machine oil. As a child, Javlon had spent hours on a stool beside the workbench, watching his father open tiny cases and lift out parts no bigger than grains of rice.
When Javlon told his father that he wanted to study engineering in another country, he expected an argument. His father had never travelled further than the regional capital, and he often said that a man should work where people knew his name. Instead, his father said nothing at all. He finished the watch he was working on, wiped his hands slowly and went to the back of the shop.
He came back holding a wooden box that Javlon had never seen before. Inside was a set of small tools, older than any in the workshop, each one carefully wrapped in cloth. "These belonged to my teacher," his father said. "He gave them to me when I left my village to learn this trade. I was seventeen. Everyone told me I was making a mistake."
He closed the box and pushed it across the bench. "You won't need them for engineering," he said, "but you will need to remember where you started."
Javlon took the box home that evening. He did not know what to say, so he said nothing either.

passages.title: Should the school shop stop selling sweet drinks?
passages.text:
This month the student council will vote on whether the school shop should stop selling sweet fizzy drinks. We asked two students for their views.
Nilufar, Grade 11: "I'm in favour of the change. The shop is the only place to buy drinks during the school day, so what it sells shapes what we drink, whether we notice it or not. Nobody is going to stop anyone bringing a drink from home. But the school shouldn't make the least healthy choice the easiest one. If the shop sold water, unsweetened tea and juice with no added sugar, most students would simply buy those instead, and after a few weeks nobody would remember the old fridge."
Akmal, Grade 10: "I agree that most of us drink too much sugar, but I don't think a ban is the answer. The shop is run partly to raise money for school trips, and fizzy drinks are what sells. If they disappear, students will buy them from the kiosk across the road, and the trip fund will lose money. I'd rather the shop put the healthy drinks at the front, made them cheaper and charged more for the sweet ones. People should learn to make good choices, not have them made for them."
The vote will take place on 14 March. Students who want to share their opinion with the council can leave a note in the box outside the library.

passages.title: The music through the wall
passages.text:
Every evening at seven, the same piece of piano music came through the wall of Madina's bedroom. It was always the same piece, and it always stopped at the same place, about a minute in, where the player made the same mistake. Then there would be a pause, and the piece would begin again from the start.
At first Madina found it almost funny. After two weeks, it was driving her mad. She was preparing for her exams, and the broken melody seemed to follow her into every page of her chemistry notes. One evening she decided to knock on the neighbour's door and politely ask whether the practice could happen earlier in the day.
The door was opened by Mr Hamidov, a retired engineer who lived alone and whom Madina knew only well enough to greet on the stairs. Behind him she could see an old piano covered in sheets of music with large handwritten notes in the margins. Before she could say anything, he apologised. "It's my granddaughter's piece," he explained. "She's playing it at her school concert next month, and I promised I'd play it with her. I haven't touched a piano for forty years."
Madina found that she no longer wanted to ask him to practise earlier. Instead, she heard herself offering to come round on Saturday. She had had piano lessons for six years as a child, and she still remembered a few things.
The following week, the piece went past the difficult place for the first time. Madina noticed that she had stopped hearing it as noise.

passages.title: The trouble with untranslatable words
passages.text:
Every few months, a list of "untranslatable words" goes around online: a word in one language for the particular sadness of a Sunday evening, another for the pleasure of reading in bed while it rains. The lists are charming, and they usually come with an implied message: that speakers of other languages experience the world in ways the rest of us cannot reach.
I am sceptical of that message, though not of the lists themselves. The fact that a language has no single word for something does not mean its speakers cannot think or feel it. English has no everyday single word for the day after tomorrow, yet nobody would argue that English speakers are confused about Wednesdays. What a missing word tells us is not what a culture is unable to perceive, but what it has not found necessary to compress into one unit of sound.
That is a less romantic conclusion, but arguably a more interesting one. Words tend to be created when an idea is needed often enough that describing it at length becomes tiresome. A community that spends long winters indoors may well develop a precise vocabulary for kinds of comfort; a community of fishermen may distinguish many kinds of wave. The vocabulary is a record of attention, not a limit on it.
This matters for anyone learning a language. Students often treat a word without a neat equivalent as an obstacle, a gap to be apologised for in translation. It is better seen as an invitation: a small window into what other people have repeatedly found worth talking about. A translator who explains such a word in a phrase has not failed. They have done precisely what speakers of the original language once did themselves, before the phrase was worn down into a single word.

passages.title: The orchard
passages.text:
When their grandmother died, the orchard passed to the three of them together, which, as Gulnora observed at the time, was like giving one violin to three people and asking them to play.
Bahodir, the eldest, wanted to sell. He had a mortgage in the city and two children whose school fees rose every year, and he spoke about the land in the patient, reasonable tone he used with difficult clients. Dilbar, the youngest, wanted to keep it exactly as it was. She drove out every weekend that first spring, though the trees needed little from her, and she would return with her car smelling of blossom and her arguments sharpened by the journey.
Gulnora, who had always been the one to settle disputes, found to her surprise that she had no opinion at all. Or rather, she had both opinions, and they cancelled each other out so precisely that she was left with a kind of silence where a decision should have been.
It was their grandmother's neighbour, an old man who had picked apricots beside her for decades, who unknowingly broke the deadlock. Meeting Gulnora at the gate one evening in June, he asked whether the family would be needing his help with the harvest as usual. She realised that she did not know how many trees there were, which ones fruited first or where the ladders were kept. Dilbar had loved the orchard; Bahodir had valued it; neither of them, she suspected, could have answered his question either.
That night she called them both. She did not propose keeping the orchard or selling it. She proposed that the three of them spend the harvest there, doing the work themselves, before anyone decided anything. Bahodir said it was sentimental. Dilbar said it was obvious. Both, somewhat to her surprise, agreed to come.

passages.title: The album and the archive
passages.text:
My grandparents own a few dozen photographs from the first thirty years of their marriage. Each one was taken deliberately, paid for when it was developed and placed in an album that came out only on particular occasions. I own several thousand photographs from the past five years, and I have looked at almost none of them twice.
It is tempting to conclude that my grandparents valued their memories more than I value mine, but I am not sure the comparison is fair. Scarcity forced them to choose, and choosing is itself a kind of remembering: to decide that this moment, rather than the hundred around it, deserves to be kept is already to have thought about what it meant. My phone's camera, by contrast, chooses nothing. It records a beautiful sunset and the receipt I photographed to claim a refund with exactly the same indifference.
The problem, then, may not be that we take too many pictures but that we have quietly handed over the work of choosing. An album was an argument about a life: these are the moments that mattered. A phone's gallery is closer to an inventory. It answers the question "what happened?" with great accuracy and the question "what was important?" not at all.
Some people respond by photographing less, which seems to me to throw away something genuinely useful. A better habit, I have found, is a small editing session at the end of each month. I choose no more than ten pictures, delete nothing, and move those ten into a separate folder with a sentence about why each one was chosen. It takes perhaps twenty minutes. The sentences are often more revealing than the pictures: reading back through a year of them, I can see what I was worried about, whom I was spending time with and what I found funny, in a way the full archive never could.

passages.title: The path in the snow
passages.text:
For as long as anyone in the neighbourhood could remember, a narrow path had run diagonally across the empty lot behind the school. Nobody had built it. It had simply appeared, worn into the grass by countless feet taking the shortest route from the bus stop to the school gate, and it had become so permanent that delivery drivers used it as a landmark.
When the district finally announced that the lot would become a small park, the architects' plans showed neat paths running along the edges and meeting at a fountain in the middle. They were elegant on paper. They were also, as a group of students pointed out at the public meeting, about ninety metres longer for anyone walking from the bus stop.
The architects' first response was that people would adapt. The students' reply was quieter but more persuasive: they brought a photograph of the lot taken from a classroom window after a light snowfall. In it, the old path was clearly visible as a single dark line, while every other part of the lot lay untouched. "You can design where you want people to walk," one of them said, "but this is where they already walk."
The plans were redrawn. The finished park has a single paved path running diagonally along exactly the line the snow had revealed, and the fountain was moved slightly to one side to make room for it. Several of the architects later said that the change had improved the design.
Planners have a name for paths like this, but the students did not need it. What they had understood was that a place carries information about how it is actually used, and that this information is easy to overlook precisely because nobody has bothered to write it down.
